textPlacement.assessment: Opening Draw / Make a mark, topic summary and full invitation preserve easy-marking chunky drawing materials, interest rather than a deadline, process over recognizable product, loose demonstration lines on separate adult paper, table protection and feedback when the child looks for it. The 12-month scribbling source label is distinguished from the 18–24 browsing placement. This bounded ordinary invitation adds no material composition, recipe or developmental outcome claim.

artContext.assessment: The exact Draw opening was read with Make a mark, its paper/crayon invitation, observation cue, Try this together CTA, three choice labels, age selector, Follow what catches their attention caption, source credit and nonprescriptive colophon. The unchanged scene depicts another household possibility while drawing materials are visible on the shelf; it does not depict a drawing accomplishment or claim that the child must reproduce the room. The child stands on the floor at a low table, pours from a modest jug with one hand and steadies the cup with the other; a caregiver is within reach and a cloth is on the table. This fits the book’s small-jug, available-help/spill-cloth and accessible-home examples. The illustration cannot establish an exact liquid amount or a universal grip; no such inference is approved. Alt text correctly places the shoe basket on the shelf’s bottom tier and describes the observed pouring rather than a generation prompt.

Checked this observed image against its frozen alt text, caption, drawing title/invitation and surrounding opening copy. No image-generation prompt or prior artwork review was used as visual evidence.

textPlacement.assessment: The topic summary can stand alone as a manageable puzzle invitation and does not specify small loose materials. The full page preserves taking apart before fitting, replacing pieces to permit repetition, the 12–14+ appendix versus around-18-month chapter context, offered minimal help, later harder puzzles and small-part supervision. It does not turn a captioned five-piece small-knob example into a universal age test.

The short surface describes movements rather than instructing access to household closures. The full perspective retains taking apart, graded challenge, differing age labels and closure variants, adult supervision for small parts, and the limit on assuming that arbitrary household objects are suitable. The held opening/closing research variant does not prevent this narrower attributed perspective from passing.

The topic row explicitly keeps adult supervision for small materials. The detail and age context accurately separate broad sorting around 18 months from photographed small-button sorting from 2 years; ordinary sock/clothing sorting is grounded in the age chart. The comparison stays nonquizzing and does not prescribe the appendix’s small-item recipe for every child in this browsing band.

Both topic contexts and the complete entry preserve shared enjoyment without skilled performance, copying the child’s rhythm or movement, family/cultural dance, action songs and short rhythmic language. Focused listening is grounded in the appendix. All ages remains expressly within the toddler activity list; no movement apparatus or readiness deadline is introduced.

All three topic rows support a bounded invitation to repeated shared reading. The detail preserves daily-life interests, diversity, changes in sentence length, careful handling and visible covers. The Montessori realistic-book preference is attributed and its occasional pretend-book exception remains visible. All ages is kept toddler-wide rather than extended to newborns.

Both topic rows and full detail preserve sounds/gestures as participation, time to reply, naturally restating the full word, showing when meaning is unclear, rich naming and silence. The appendix’s cultural qualification on eye contact is public, rather than overridden by the less qualified chapter wording. No language milestone or correction drill is added.

Both topic summaries retain familiar naming and optional identical matching without introducing small replicas there. The full page distinguishes identical from later similar matching, keeps theme and source age labels separate, avoids turning a wrong match into a test, and carries supervision wherever small real/replica objects enter the prose. The over-3 formal third-period reference is contextual, not a new procedure for this band.

The topic summary is an attributed supervised-material perspective. Full detail preserves watercolor brush/jar/one-color paper-and-cloth context, chunky chalk and large-surface movement, and easel standing readiness. It correctly describes thick paint in a cup rather than a measured cup of paint, keeps younger-toddler supervision public and avoids manufacturing a chronological readiness label.

The topic summary retains shared supervision. The detail accurately describes the glue application/turn/press movement and a few large shapes, and clay/play dough/kinetic sand as material exploration with simple tools. Small/sharp-object supervision remains explicit, the 16–18+/18-month source labels are distinct from browsing, and the hot-water recipe and storage claims are not imported.

The standalone topic invitation confines itself to looking/listening and ordinary discoveries. Full detail preserves available time, child pace, wondering together and alternatives without private outdoor space. It does not adopt the surrounding source’s water play, collection recipes, weather imperatives or climbing examples. The generic materials readiness wording is awkward but makes no unsupported setup or deadline claim.

The topic row stays an attributed perspective on current movement. Full detail preserves indoor space permitting, the outdoor rationale for ball play, and the existence of different equipment ages/readiness rather than prescribing a combined activity progression. The source’s balance-bike timing variants remain unmerged; no apparatus construction, elevation or adult positioning instruction is added.

issues.finding: The interpretation of pretend play as processing experienced daily life is on PDF 103, where Davies places its beginning around 2.5+ years. The frozen 18–24-month entry uses that interpretation with a current-child pretend cue but supplies only a generic age-guidance note and cites PDF 104, which discusses artistic creativity. PDF 71 separately supports unaged home open-ended/imaginative play; that support does not make the more specific PDF 103 interpretation and age context disappear.
issues.requiredCorrection: Keep the unaged PDF 71–72 home-play perspective, but either remove the PDF 103 processing interpretation and its associated pretend cue, or add the exact around-2.5+ source framing as later context with a corrected PDF 103–104 reference. Preserve its distinction from this editorial 18–24 placement and do not turn it into a deadline. Attribute only source examples, or use the broader source-supported wording about daily-life scenarios.

The unaged home-toy examples can support a narrow perspective; the held block example alone is not grounds for excluding the entry.
